newsitem.title: UK: UK gilts this week - US jobs, rate meeting top bill.
newsitem.headline: UK gilts this week - US jobs, rate meeting top bill.

text.p: U.S. non-farm payroll data will wrestle with the UK monthly monetary meeting to capture the attention of the gilts market this week, analysts said.
"The monetary meeting has the ability to surprise, but there is a lot of uncertainty over the U.S. payroll data. That could turn out to be the week's main event," said Kevin Adams at BZW.

Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and Governor of the Bank of England Eddie George meet on Wednesday. Only a handful of economists expect a rate cut to follow the meeting, but even fewer are prepared to rule one out altogether.
A poll conducted by Reuters found 13 out of a total of 20 economists questioned said rates would be left on hold.
But if Clarke confounds the forecasters and cuts rates again, he can bank on an adverse reaction from gilts.
"Gilts will not like it. The curve will steepen and not just because short-end (yields) shifts down. The long end will almost certainly sell off," said Adams, a gilts analyst.

Steven Andrew, analyst at Merrill Lynch, agreed gilts would not like a rate cut with little economic justification. "Clarke does not have enough ammunition this time around with all the recent data showing signs of renewed growth in the second half."
"There is even less evidence that could be used to justifiy a cut than at the last meeting when rates were left on hold."
Although retail sales fell in July and broad money supply growth eased, other data suggested a lively economic recovery.
If Clarke is still looking for evidence to press for a rate cut, Monday's data brought him cold comfort.
The August PMI showed clear signs that consumer spending was feeding though to the manufacturing side, the weakest link in the economic recovery to date.
And the Bank of England said narrow money supply growth shot up to 7.5 percent in August from 7.1 in July.
The rest of the week offers little domestic data until industrial production on Friday, forecast to show a smart recovery in manufacturing output in July.
But the U.S. August non-farm payroll, also due on Friday, is likely to steal the limelight.
It is forecast to show a meaty rise of 244,000. Traders say the risks are on the upside and a higher figure will send Treasuries into a spin.
"The market is expecting a big figure so a 200,000-plus number is not going to do too much damage," said one gilts trader at a gilts market-maker.
"But the U.S. market is still looking vulnerable, even after Friday's sell-off, so it will get nervous before the release."
Last Friday, U.S. Treasuries plunged and pulled Europe down, too, after the release of a much stronger-than-expected Chicago purchasing managers report.
The yield spread between gilts and Bunds widened marginally on Monday, but it should stay steady at around 165 basis point this week, analysts said.
But BZW's Adams said any more negative comments concerning European Economic and Monetary Union may in time play into the hands of the UK market.
Any data or remarks suggesting key European countries will fail to meet the Maastricht convergence criteria could give the UK some safe-haven status, he said.
"There must be some spread premium in the official British line that the UK can stay out of the EMU and still have all the benefits," Adams said.

And, barring any surprises on rates, the UK yield curve should stay steady, although the five-year area remains vulnerable. Five-year gilts are still overpriced with the five-to-10-year spread still at record levels around 70 basis points, analysts said.
